newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia may beat jobs forecast - Treasury.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia may beat jobs forecast - Treasury.

text.p: The Australian Treasury said even a conservative interpretation of recent data showed Australia will meet or exceed revised forecasts for jobs growth.

The Treasury also said its business investment forecast, which it recently revised up, was quite conservative and its forecast for healthy GDP growth took into account the possibility of businesses running down their inventories.

The jobs picture was clouded by the understatement of growth caused by the Australian Bureau of Statistics' changing to telephone interviewing for its labour force data, the Treasury said in its quarterly Roundup commentary dated February 6.

"With final estimates of the cumulative impact remaining in some doubt, caution suggests that recent outcomes should be interpreted as being broadly consistent with the budget and mid-year outlook forecasts, though pointing to the possibility of some upside risk to those forecasts," it said.

January data issued on Thursday showed an acceleration in jobs growth, even without allowing for the understatement caused by the change to telephone interviewing, which the bureau says is reducing its jobs-growth estimates by 6,000 to 9,000 a month.
The government's mid-year outlook issued last month forecast average employment for the year to June 1997 would be 1.5-percent higher than the previous fiscal year.

But January published employment estimates were already 1.3 -ercent above their June level.Treasurer Peter Costello said on Thursday that if one allowed for the methodological change, the year's forecast had already been met.

"The acceleration in employment growth also supports an assesment that the weakness of employment growth in the first half of 1996 reflected -- in addition to the effects of earlier increases in real labour costs -- a correction to employment growth during 1995 which was in excess of that implied by underlying fundamental determinants," Treasury said.
While 1996 jobs growth slowed, the rate of businesses' inventory accumulation generally grew, raising concerns the economy would return to lower growth rates as firms sought to run down their stocks.
But the Treasury anticipated such a rundown and said it had allowed for one in its forecast for 3.5- percent GDP growth in 1996/97.

"Unless the current estimate (of inventories) is also revised down significantly, or unless there have been structural changes which have brought the earlier improvements in stock-handling practices to an end, it is likely that the large contribution to growth evident in the September quarter will be unwound in coming quarters," it said.
"Such an unwinding is reflected in the revised forecasts."
The Treasury in January revised up its 1996/97 business investment forecast to 17 percent from the August forecast of 14 percent, offsetting a weaker outlook for private consumption.
But on Thursday, it said even that upward revision was conservative.
"Indeed, based on previous experience, the revised forecast is quite conservative," it said.
